terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see the callout book taken apart into lines and parts, the hours added up and a line put back together.

tasks.title: How many words
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `callout_book.py`, write a function called `word_count` that takes a radio message and gives back how many words it has, as a whole number. Spaces only separate the words, however many there are in a row, and so do a line end or spaces at the start or the end. For `message` it gives back `9`. Print what it gives back for `message`.

Check calls `word_count` with messages of its own, some with two spaces in a row and some with a line end, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on splitting at spaces.
Split the message into a list of its words.
Give back how many items that list has.
Try it on a message with two spaces in a row.
hints: Splitting at one space gives an empty text between two spaces in a row, and that empty text is counted as a word.
`split` with nothing in its brackets splits at any run of spaces, tabs and line ends, and leaves nothing empty at the ends. `len` counts the items of a list.

tasks.title: The book, line by line
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, write a function called `book_lines` that takes the whole book as one text and gives back a list of its lines, in order, without their line ends. The line end after the last line does not make an empty line, a book typed on Windows has `\r\n` at the end of each line, and an empty book gives back an empty list. Print what it gives back for `book`.

Check calls `book_lines` with books of its own, one typed on Windows and one with no line end after its last line, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on lines.
Find the method that splits a text into its lines.
Give back what it gives back.
Print it, and look at the end of the list for an empty text.
hints: Splitting at `\n` leaves an empty text after the last line end, and leaves the `\r` of a Windows line end on each line.
Text has a method made for lines: it splits at every kind of line end and adds no empty line at the end.

tasks.title: One callout in its parts
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write a function called `callout_parts` that takes one line of the book and gives back a list of its parts: the text between the semicolons, each without the spaces at its start and end. For the first line of `book` it gives back `['14 Nov', 'Carn Dubh', '3 hours', '8 crew']`. The parts are text, the numbers too. Print what it gives back for the first line of the book.

Check calls `callout_parts` with lines of its own, some with spaces around a semicolon and some with none, and one with a line end, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on splitting at a separator.
Split the line at each semicolon.
Make a new list with each part stripped.
Give back the new list.
hints: Splitting at a semicolon and a space misses a semicolon with no space after it, and splitting at a semicolon alone keeps the spaces around each part.
Split at the semicolon alone, then go through the parts and add each one, stripped, to a new list.
The shape is `parts = []`, then `for part in line.split(";"):` with `parts.append(part.strip())`, and `return parts`.

tasks.title: The hours added up
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, write a function called `total_hours` that takes a list of lines of the book and gives back the hours of all of them added up, as a whole number, or `0` for an empty list. The hours are the third part of a line, such as `3 hours` or `1 hour`. For the lines of `book` it gives back `20`. You may use your `callout_parts`. Print what it gives back for the lines of `book`.

Check calls `total_hours` with lines of its own, some with more than nine hours, and looks at what it gives back. It gives your file its own `callout_parts` and `book_lines` first, so a mistake in Task 2 or 3 does not count here.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on numbers inside text.
Start a total at 0 and go through the lines.
Take the third part of each line, and the number from the start of it.
Turn that number into a whole number and add it to the total.
hints: `int()` turns text into a number only when the text is a whole number and nothing else: `int("3 hours")` stops with a `ValueError`.
Split the part at its spaces: the first word is the number. Its first letter alone is not, when the number has two digits.
The shape is `total = total + int(callout_parts(line)[2].split()[0])` inside `for line in lines:`, after `total = 0`.

tasks.title: Put the right hill back
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 5`, write a function called `with_hill` that takes one line of the book and the name of a hill, and gives back a new line with that hill in place of the one the line had, all its parts stripped and joined with a semicolon and a space between each. For the third line of `book` and `"Carn Dubh"` it gives back `02 Dec; Carn Dubh; 12 hours; 10 crew`. Print what it gives back for that line and `"Carn Dubh"`.

Check calls `with_hill` with lines and hills of its own and looks at what it gives back. It gives your file its own `callout_parts` first, so a mistake in Task 3 does not count here.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on joining.
Take the line apart into its parts.
Put the new hill in the place of the second part.
Join the parts back into one text and give it back.
hints: The parts are a list, so one of them can be replaced by its position, and the hill is at position 1.
`join` is called on the text that goes between the parts, and the list of parts goes in its brackets. It adds nothing at the ends.
The shape is `parts = callout_parts(line)`, then `parts[1] = hill` and `return "; ".join(parts)`.
